title: Deterministic route resolver for geo-tier + model-version stickiness
creator: Sofia Patel
description:
Background: We currently support multiple routing dimensions (region preference, customer tier, version pinning and simple fallback to model variants), but behavior is emergent and non-deterministic under concurrent changes (rollouts, region outages, autoscale-driven capacity shifts). This causes user-visible variance: sessions can flip between model variants mid-conversation during a canary rollout or when region failover triggers. Goal: implement a deterministic route resolution algorithm that composes region selection, tier routing, and model-version pinning with stable session affinity and graceful degrade to compatible variants. It must be: 1) deterministic given the same request metadata and config; 2) stable for sticky sessions (TTL-based affinity); 3) respectful of explicit pinning rules and rollout policies; 4) fast to evaluate in the request path; 5) debuggable with trace metadata and deterministic tie-break logs.

Proposed approach summary:
- Route key and priority vector: construct a canonical priority vector for each request that includes explicit pins (route.version_pin), customer tier (route.tier), region hints (client_region, requested_region), and rollout policy buckets (canary/A-B). The resolver will sort candidates using a deterministic comparator (priority vector then hash tie-breaker). 
- Stable affinity: introduce a session-affinity token (session_id or allocation returned by cache) with TTL. Affinity binds to a specific route tuple (region, tier, model_version). Rebinding only occurs when the bound candidate is unavailable or the TTL expires.
- Version pin semantics: explicit version_pin always wins unless unavailable. If a pinned version is not available in the selected region/tier, the resolver attempts cross-region compatible variants using a compatibility matrix (e.g., model_v2_q4 -> degrade to model_v2_q8 or v1-compatible), honoring policy that prevents cross-major-version fallback unless allow_major_fallback flag enabled.
- Canary/A-B handling: requests assigned to a canary bucket by rollout policy receive route priority that prefers canary instances. The allocation remains sticky for the session TTL. For A/B experiments, maintain deterministic hashing (user_id or session_id) to ensure consistent exposure.
- Tie-breaker: when multiple candidates have equivalent priority, use a stable 64-bit FNV-like hash of (customer_id|session_id|request_id) mod candidate_count to pick an index — ensures deterministic selection across replicas.
- Backpressure and graceful degrade: if target candidate is overloaded, mark as degraded and compute next-best candidate preserving affinity semantics. Provide metrics for degrade-count and degrade-latency.

Design details and data model:
- New config fields: route.priority_order (list), route.allow_major_fallback (bool), affinity.ttl_seconds (int), fallback.compatibility_profile (string).
- Resolver input: canonicalized request metadata keys: customer_id, session_id, client_region, requested_region, tier, version_pin, rollout_bucket.
- Output: selected_region, selected_tier, selected_model_version, affinity_token, resolution_trace (string id for debugging).
- Logs/Tracing: emit deterministic trace with chosen vector and tie-break hash. Surface resolver decisions in Console rollout traces and request-level debug mode.

Acceptance criteria (must pass before rolling to 100%):
- Unit tests for comparator and hash tie-breaker with synthetic candidate sets demonstrate deterministic outcome across 10000 seeds.
- Integration tests: simulated canary rollouts (10% canary traffic) show at least 99.9% session stickiness over 30m window.
- Chaos test: when a region becomes unavailable, 100% of requests currently bound to unavailable candidates recover to a valid fallback within 500ms and preserve session-affinity semantics when possible.
- Performance: resolver must add <0.25ms p50 latency to request path in benchmarked environment (p95 <1ms).
- Observability: Console shows resolver decision reason for 100% of sampled requests and degrade metrics appear in dashboards.

Rollout plan:
1) Feature branch + unit tests (ENG-35910). 2) Internal dogfood on devcluster with feature flag (1 week). 3) Small canary across 1-2 customers with targeted sessions (2 weeks). 4) Incremental ramp with monitoring checks for degrade and error rates. 5) Full rollout.

Risks and tradeoffs:
- Increasing resolver complexity may add CPU overhead; mitigate with a compiled comparator table and memoization for frequent customers.
- Strict pin semantics may cause capacity shortages; will expose metrics and implement automatic fallback policy overrides for high-severity customer incidents.
- Cross-region fallbacks can increase latency; ensure allow_major_fallback defaults to false and only used with explicit opt-in.

Open questions:
- TTL default value for affinity (30m vs 24h) — initial proposal: 30m for interactive features, 24h for streaming/long-lived sessions.
- How to represent compatibility profiles for third-party models (need a small schema).

Implementation notes:
- Primary work: resolver library (go), console traces (backend + UI), config schema, tests, rollout gating.
- PRs:
  - library: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/PR-4512
  - console traces: github.com/redwood-inference/console/PR-987

Non-goals: global balancing changes (we will not change autoscaler logic here), nor deep model-compatibility inference (we rely on curated compatibility profiles).
